newsitem.title: USA: Kentucky says refunds 'doable' with some juggling.
newsitem.headline: Kentucky says refunds 'doable' with some juggling.

text.p: Kentucky may have to juggle other projects to pay $240 million in court-ordered intangibles tax refunds, but should be able to make the payments without endangering its bond rating, a state official said Monday.

The Kentucky Supreme Court ruled Jan 30 that the state's intangibles tax law was unconstitutional because it taxed the stock of in-state and out-of-state companies at different rates. The court ordered refunds that could total $240 million to about 100,000 taxpayers.
"It'll be a hardship," said William Hintz of the governor's budget office.

However, he said, "It is doable and obviously we will make due on it, but it will not be without altering plans and causing some adjustments on what we'd like to do and the timetables we'd like to do it on."
He did not say what other projects may have to be delayed, because the state has not yet decided which revenues will be used for the refunds.
"We have a number of options. We're reviewing those," Hintz said.
Kentucky has a $200 million budget reserve trust it can draw on in emergencies, and that is "a likely candidate" Hintze said.
State law limits expenditures from the fund to $50 million a year. The limit could be raised by the legislature, although "We would be uncomfortable with cleaning it out."
Due to the state's strong economy, revenues for the year have exceeded projections by about $60 million, so some of that could be used, Hintze said.
He said the state also has other "creative financing" options it is reviewing.
Revenue officials said they expect to begin paying the refunds by the end of the fiscal year June 30.

Hintze said he did not anticpate any effect on the state's credit rating and that the refund order, which covers two years worth of payments, was smaller than the $341 million the state had feared it could be ordered to repay.
"This is not an unexpected event. While it's not a welcome one, from the prospect of trying to manage state resources, it is doable," Hintze said.
State officials had expected the intangibles tax law would be struck down since the U.S. Supreme Court struck down a similar law in North Carolina.
